```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

The dynamic part of a ctsem model is a set of differential equations, and its
parameters are rates of change per unit of time. This vignette explains how to
read them: what the auto and cross effects mean, how to tell whether the
processes are stable, how fast they change, what the effects are over a given
time interval, and where the processes settle. The first sections use drift
matrices with chosen values, and the last applies the same steps to a fitted
model.

# One process

A single latent process $\eta$ follows

$$
\mathrm{d}\eta(t) = \big(a\,\eta(t) + b\big)\,\mathrm{d}t + g\,\mathrm{d}W(t)
$$

- $a$ is the auto effect, the `DRIFT` matrix. When $\eta$ is one unit above
  its equilibrium, it changes by $a$ units per unit of time. When $a$ is
  negative the process returns towards an equilibrium, faster the more
  negative it is. When $a$ is zero it has no equilibrium and wanders as a
  random walk. When $a$ is positive a deviation grows.
- $b$ is the continuous time intercept, `CINT`. With $a < 0$ the equilibrium
  is $-b/a$.
- $g$ is the size of the random shocks, `DIFFUSION`. With $a < 0$ the
  process varies around its equilibrium with variance $g^2 / (-2a)$.

Over a time interval $\Delta t$ the process is an autoregression with
coefficient $e^{a \Delta t}$. A deviation from equilibrium halves in
$\log(2) / |a|$ units of time, the half-life. The units are those of the time
column in the data. With time in days, $a = -0.1$ gives a half-life of about 7
days. The same process with time in weeks has $a = -0.7$.

```{r one-process}
intervals <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)
onep <- expand.grid(interval = intervals, a = c(-0.1, -0.5, -1))
onep$autoregression <- exp(onep$a * onep$interval)
ggplot(onep, aes(interval, autoregression, colour = factor(a))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + theme_bw() +
  labs(x = 'time interval', y = 'autoregression', colour = 'auto effect a')
log(2) / c(0.1, 0.5, 1)   # half-lives
```

# Two processes

With more than one process, $a$ becomes the drift matrix $A$, $b$ the vector
of intercepts, and $g$ a matrix $G$ whose product $GG^\top$ is the covariance
of the shocks:

$$
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol\eta(t) = \big(A\,\boldsymbol\eta(t) + \mathbf b\big)\,\mathrm{d}t + G\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf W(t)
$$

The diagonal of $A$ holds the auto effects. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$
is the cross effect of process $j$ on the rate of change of process $i$. In
ctsem's parameter names, `drift_eta2_eta1` is the effect of `eta1` on `eta2`.

A cross effect is a rate. What a discrete time model would estimate as a
cross-lagged coefficient for an interval $\Delta t$ is an entry of the matrix
exponential $e^{A \Delta t}$, which depends on the whole drift matrix and on
the interval. In this system `eta1` drives `eta2`:

```{r two-process}
A <- matrix(c(-0.4,  0,
               0.3, -0.2), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c('eta1', 'eta2'), c('eta1', 'eta2')))
A

discrete <- function(A, intervals) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(intervals, function(dt) {
    E <- expm::expm(A * dt)
    data.frame(interval = dt, value = c(E),
      effect = paste(rep(colnames(A), each = nrow(A)), '->',
        rep(rownames(A), ncol(A))))
  }))
}
d2 <- discrete(A, seq(0, 20, by = 0.1))
ggplot(d2, aes(interval, value, colour = effect)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + theme_bw() +
  labs(x = 'time interval', y = 'discrete time effect')
```

The cross effect of `eta1` on `eta2` is zero over no time, rises as the change
in `eta1` passes into `eta2`, and falls as both return to equilibrium. Its
largest value is at an interval of about 3.5. A cross-lagged coefficient from a
study with one interval between waves is one point on this curve, so two
studies with different intervals can find quite different coefficients for the
same process. A continuous time model fitted to either should give the same
drift matrix.

# Stability

A system is stable when every disturbance fades and the processes return to
their equilibrium. For one process that means $a < 0$. With more processes it
depends on the whole drift matrix. The system is stable when every eigenvalue
of $A$ has a negative real part. Negative auto effects do not
ensure this, and a positive auto effect does not rule it out. For two processes
the condition is the same as a negative sum of the auto effects together with
a positive determinant of $A$.

Three drift matrices show this:

```{r stability}
drifts <- list(
  'negative auto effects, stable' =
    matrix(c(-0.5, 0.2, 0.2, -0.5), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE),
  'negative auto effects, unstable' =
    matrix(c(-0.5, 0.7, 0.7, -0.5), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE),
  'a positive auto effect, stable' =
    matrix(c(0.1, -0.6, 0.6, -0.5), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE))
lapply(drifts, function(A) eigen(A)$values)
```

The second matrix has the same auto effects as the first, but the two
processes push each other up strongly enough that a disturbance grows. Its
eigenvalues are 0.2 and -1.2, and the positive one makes it unstable. The
third has a positive auto effect for the first process, which on its own would
grow, but the second process pulls it back. Its eigenvalues are complex with
real part -0.2, so it is stable and oscillates. The trajectories after a
disturbance of one unit in the first process, with no further shocks
($e^{At}$ times the disturbance):

```{r trajectories}
trajectory <- function(A, start, times) {
  out <- t(sapply(times, function(t) expm::expm(A * t) %*% start))
  data.frame(time = times, eta1 = out[, 1], eta2 = out[, 2])
}
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(drifts), function(n) {
  p <- trajectory(drifts[[n]], start = c(1, 0), times = seq(0, 15, by = 0.1))
  rbind(data.frame(system = n, time = p$time, process = 'eta1', value = p$eta1),
        data.frame(system = n, time = p$time, process = 'eta2', value = p$eta2))
}))
paths$system <- factor(paths$system, levels = names(drifts))
ggplot(paths, aes(time, value, colour = process)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = 'grey60') +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~system, scales = 'free_y') +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = 'bottom')
```

An unstable system has no equilibrium to return to, so it has no stationary
mean or variance. ctsem reports the asymptotic matrices described below as
`NaN` for it. In a fitted model, an estimated drift matrix close to
instability often means a slow process, such as a trend, that the model does
not describe separately.

# How fast

The eigenvalues also give the time scale. Each real eigenvalue $\lambda$
belongs to a combination of the processes that returns to equilibrium at rate
$\lambda$, with half-life $\log(2) / |\lambda|$. The eigenvalue with the real
part nearest zero is the slowest, and sets how long the system as a whole
takes to settle. In the first system above each auto effect alone would give a
half-life of `r round(log(2) / 0.5, 1)`. The processes support each other, and
the slowest combination has a half-life of
`r round(log(2) / 0.3, 1)`:

```{r halflife}
ev <- eigen(drifts[[1]])$values
log(2) / abs(Re(ev))
```

Complex eigenvalues mean oscillation. The period is $2\pi / |\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda|$,
and the amplitude halves in $\log(2) / |\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda|$. For the third
system:

```{r oscillation}
ev <- eigen(drifts[[3]])$values
c(period = 2 * pi / abs(Im(ev[1])), amplitude_halflife = log(2) / abs(Re(ev[1])))
```

A single process can only oscillate when it is modelled with a second, unseen
process, its rate of change. `ctModelHigherOrder()` adds one to a model.

# Where the processes settle

A stable system fluctuates around its equilibrium with a stationary
distribution, within each subject. Its mean is $-A^{-1}\mathbf b$, and its
covariance $\Sigma$ solves $A\Sigma + \Sigma A^\top + GG^\top = 0$. ctsem
reports these as `asymCINT` and `asymDIFFUSIONcov` (and the correlations as
`asymDIFFUSIONcor`) in `summary(fit)$parmatrices` and `ctSummaryMatrices()`.
For the first system with intercepts of 1 and 0 and independent unit shocks:

```{r asymptotic}
A <- drifts[[1]]
b <- c(1, 0)
Q <- diag(2)                                    # G G'
-solve(A, b)                                    # equilibrium
I <- diag(2)
matrix(-solve(kronecker(I, A) + kronecker(A, I), c(Q)), 2, 2)   # stationary covariance
```

The second process has no intercept of its own, but it settles above zero
because the first pushes it up.

# Comparing effects across processes

A cross effect is the change in process $i$ per unit of process $j$, so it
depends on the units of both. When the processes are on different scales, the
effects are easier to compare standardised by the stationary standard
deviations, as the change in standard deviations of $i$ per standard deviation
of $j$. `ctDiscretePars(fit, standardise = TRUE)` gives the discrete time
effects on that scale, and `ctNetwork()` the network of effects at one
interval.

# A fitted model

The README fits a model to the daily milk yield and fat percentage of 53 cows,
with time in days. The same fit:

```{r milk-fit, results = 'hide'}
data(milkman_rdm1, package = 'doBy')
milk <- data.frame(
  cow   = milkman_rdm1$cowno,
  day   = milkman_rdm1$dfc,
  yield = as.numeric(scale(milkman_rdm1$my)),
  fat   = as.numeric(scale(milkman_rdm1$fatpct)))

model <- ctModel(LAMBDA = diag(2), manifestNames = c('yield', 'fat'),
  latentNames = c('yield', 'fat'), time = 'day', id = 'cow')
fit <- ctFit(milk, model, cores = 2)
```

The estimated drift matrix, with each row the process that changes:

```{r milk-drift}
est <- ctSummaryMatrices(fit)$estimate
est$DRIFT
eigen(est$DRIFT)$values
log(2) / abs(eigen(est$DRIFT)$values)    # half-lives in days
```

Both eigenvalues are negative, so the two processes are stable together. The
slower combination has a half-life of about two months, longer than either
auto effect would give alone. The two cross effects form a loop that keeps a
deviation going: higher fat lowers yield, and lower yield raises fat. Each draw of the fit's parameters gives its own
drift matrix, and so its own eigenvalues, which gives their uncertainty:

```{r milk-eigen-draws}
draws <- ctExtract(fit)$pop_DRIFT
slowest <- apply(draws, 1, function(A) max(Re(eigen(A)$values)))
quantile(slowest, c(.025, .5, .975))
quantile(log(2) / abs(slowest), c(.025, .5, .975))   # its half-life in days
mean(slowest < 0)                                     # share of draws that are stable
```

The discrete time effects, over intervals from a day to five months. The time
range should cover the time scale of the processes, which ctsem cannot choose
for you:

```{r milk-discrete, fig.height = 4.6}
ctDiscretePars(fit, times = seq(0, 150, by = 1), plot = TRUE)
```

`summary()` of the same output gives each curve's peak, the interval at which
it peaks, and the interval at which it has fallen to half the peak:

```{r milk-discrete-summary}
dp <- ctDiscretePars(fit, times = seq(0, 150, by = 1))
s <- summary(dp)
s[s$quantity %in% c('peak', 'peaktime', 'halftime'),
  c('row', 'col', 'quantity', 'estimate', '2.5%', '97.5%')]
```

A higher fat percentage is followed by a lower yield, most strongly after about
six weeks, when one unit of fat (the data are standardised, so about one
standard deviation) goes with a yield about 0.29 lower. The effect of yield on
fat is smaller and its interval includes zero.

Within a cow, yield and fat vary together in the long run as well, through the
cross effects and through shocks that affect both at once:

```{r milk-asym}
est$DIFFUSIONcor          # correlation of the shocks
est$asymDIFFUSIONcor      # stationary correlation within a cow
```

# State dependent dynamics

When a drift cell is an expression of the latent states, for example an auto
effect that grows with the level of the process, the drift matrix differs from
state to state, and so do its eigenvalues and the discrete time effects.
Functions that report them then evaluate the model at one state and say which.
`ctPhasePortrait()` and `ctStateDependencePlot()` show how the dynamics change
across states.
